rows.stem:
In an electrochemical cell, the following reaction takes place :
\(\mathrm{2Cu^{+}\,(aq) + Zn\,(s) \rightarrow 2Cu\,(s) + Zn^{2+}\,(aq)}\)
\(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{cell}} = 1{\cdot}28\) V
As the reaction progresses, what will happen to the overall voltage of the cell ?
rows.solution:
As the cell runs, zinc is consumed and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) accumulates while \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) is used up. By the Nernst equation,
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cu^+}]^2}\)
the reaction quotient rises on both counts — its numerator grows and its denominator shrinks — so the logarithm increases and the cell voltage FALLS. It keeps falling until the quotient reaches the equilibrium constant, at which point \(E_{cell} = 0\) and the cell is dead. So the voltage decreases as \([\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]\) increases.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Out of \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) ions, the one which is colourless in aqueous solution is :
[Atomic number : Fe = 26, Sc = 21, Cr = 24, Co = 27]
rows.solution: Colour in these ions comes from a d-d transition, which needs a partly filled d subshell. Iron(III) is \(3d^5\), chromium(III) is \(3d^3\) and cobalt(III) is \(3d^6\) — all partly filled, so all three are coloured in solution. Scandium has 21 electrons, so \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\): the d subshell is completely EMPTY, no electron is available to promote, no visible light is absorbed, and the solution is colourless.

rows.stem: Hoffmann Bromamide degradation reaction is given by :
rows.solution:
Hofmann bromamide degradation converts an AMIDE into a primary amine with one carbon fewer, using bromine in aqueous alkali:
\(\mathrm{ArCONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ArNH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
So the compound that GIVES the reaction is the amide, \(\mathrm{ArCONH_2}\). The amine \(\mathrm{ArNH_2}\) is its product, not its substrate; \(\mathrm{ArNO_2}\) is reduced rather than degraded; and \(\mathrm{ArCH_2NH_2}\) is an amine already.

rows.stem: In the Haworth structure of the following carbohydrate, various carbon atoms have been numbered. The anomeric carbon is numbered as :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the carbohydrate exists ONLY as a drawn Haworth projection and the stem names no compound at all. A six-membered pyranose ring drawn in perspective with the ring oxygen at the upper right; five of the ring carbons carry printed numerals, and each ring carbon carries an H and an OH (or, at one position, a CH2OH) above or below the ring plane. The numbering the question turns on exists nowhere but the drawing, so the row is unanswerable without it, and the options are bare numerals so nothing in the text can substitute. Deliberately described rather than named: naming the sugar or saying which ring position sits next to the ring oxygen would state the answer. Page idx 4.
rows.solution: The anomeric carbon is the one that becomes a new stereocentre when the open chain closes into its cyclic hemiacetal form — that is, the carbonyl carbon of the open chain. In the Haworth projection of an ALDOSE such as glucose that is C-1, the carbon carrying both the ring oxygen and a hydroxyl group. Numbered as printed, the anomeric carbon is 1. (In a ketose such as fructose the carbonyl is at C-2, and that is the anomeric carbon instead.)

rows.stem: The value of Henry's constant \(\mathrm{K_H}\) is :

options.label: A
options.text: greater for gases with higher solubility

options.label: B
options.text: greater for gases with lower solubility

options.label: D
options.text: not related to the solubility of gases

rows.solution: Henry's law is \(p = K_H x\), so for a given partial pressure the mole fraction dissolved is \(x = p/K_H\). The constant sits in the DENOMINATOR, so a LARGE \(K_H\) means a SMALL amount dissolved. Henry's constant is therefore greater for gases of LOWER solubility. It also varies with temperature — rising as the temperature rises, which is why gases are less soluble in warm water — so it is certainly not constant for all gases nor unrelated to solubility.

rows.stem: Out of the following statements, the **incorrect** statement is :

options.label: A
options.text: La is actually an element of transition series.

options.label: B
options.text: Zr and Hf have almost identical atomic radii because of lanthanoid contraction.

options.label: C
options.text: Ionic radius decreases from \(\mathrm{La^{3+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu^{3+}}\) ion.

rows.solution:
Three of the statements are correct. Lanthanum, \([\mathrm{Xe}]5d^1 6s^2\), does belong to the transition series proper. Zirconium and hafnium have almost identical atomic radii because lanthanoid contraction cancels the expected increase. And the ionic radius does decrease steadily from \(\mathrm{La^{3+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu^{3+}}\), which is what lanthanoid contraction IS.

The incorrect statement is that lanthanoids are radioactive. Only promethium is; the rest are stable. It is the ACTINOIDS that are radioactive without exception.

rows.stem: Out of 2-Bromobutane, 1-Bromobutane, 2-Bromopropane and 1-Bromopropane, the molecule which is chiral in nature is :
rows.solution: A molecule is chiral if it has a carbon carrying four different groups. In 1-bromopropane and 1-bromobutane the carbon bearing the bromine also carries two hydrogens. In 2-bromopropane that carbon carries two identical methyl groups. In 2-bromobutane the second carbon carries \(-\mathrm{Br}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) — four different groups — so 2-bromobutane is the chiral molecule.

rows.stem:
In the given reaction sequence, the structure of Y would be :
Aniline \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{HCl},\ 0-5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2}}\) X \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}}\) Y
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — every one of the four options is a DRAWN benzene ring and the option list carries no words at all: (A) a ring bearing OH, (B) a bare ring, (C) a ring bearing NO2, (D) a ring bearing N2+Cl−. The stem's reactant is likewise drawn (a ring bearing NH2, captioned '(Aniline)') with the two reagent arrows above it. I NAMED the four drawn options rather than describing them, because naming is a lossless reading here and does NOT state the answer — the question tests whether a diazonium salt warmed with ethanol is reduced to the arene, and a student still has to know that. The stem's own reagents are transcribed as printed; only the drawn aniline is replaced by its printed caption. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
Sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid at \(0-5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises aniline, so X is benzenediazonium chloride. Ethanol then REDUCES the diazonium group, supplying a hydrogen atom in its place while nitrogen leaves as gas; the ethanol is itself oxidised to ethanal.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
So Y is benzene. Water in place of ethanol would have given phenol, which is the distractor.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: The product of the oxidation of \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) with \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) in alkaline medium is :
rows.solution:
In ALKALINE medium permanganate is a strong enough oxidant to take iodide past iodine to the iodate ion:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{I^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{IO_3^-} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\)
The word alkaline is what decides it: in ACIDIC medium the same reagents give iodine, \(\mathrm{I_2}\), which is the distractor offered here.

rows.stem: Polyhalogen compounds have wide application in industries and agriculture. DDT is also a very important polyhalogen compound. It is a :
rows.solution: DDT is a NON-BIODEGRADABLE insecticide. Its chlorinated structure resists breakdown by soil and water organisms, so it persists in the environment for years and accumulates up the food chain in fatty tissue — the reason its use has been banned or restricted in most countries. It is not a greenhouse gas and certainly not a fertiliser.

rows.stem: What amount of electric charge is required for the reduction of 1 mole of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) into \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ?
rows.solution:
Work from the change in oxidation state. In \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) manganese is \(+7\); in \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) it is \(+2\). Each manganese therefore gains FIVE electrons:
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)
One mole needs five moles of electrons, so the charge required is 5 F. Reduction only as far as \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) would need 3 F, which is the other version of this question.

rows.stem: Alkenes are formed by heating alcohols with conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\). The first step in the reaction is :
rows.solution: Acid catalysed dehydration runs in three steps, and the question asks for the FIRST. The alcohol's oxygen uses a lone pair to pick up a proton from the acid, giving the protonated alcohol; this step is fast and reversible. Only then does that protonated alcohol lose water, in the slow step, to give the carbocation — so the carbocation comes second, not first. Elimination of water is the same slow step described the other way round, and no ester is involved at all in the alkene-forming path.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl gives \(\mathrm{H_2}\) at cathode and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) at anode.
Reason (R) : Chlorine has higher oxidation potential than \(\mathrm{H_2O}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride does give hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode, so the Assertion is true.

The Reason is false as stated. Oxidising water needs \(1.23\) V and oxidising chloride \(1.36\) V, so on standard potentials WATER has the higher oxidation potential and oxygen should appear. What actually decides the outcome is the large OVERPOTENTIAL for oxygen evolution on a real electrode, which raises the effective voltage oxygen needs above the voltage chlorine needs. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false — and the real explanation is kinetic, not thermodynamic.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Cuprous salts are diamagnetic.
Reason (R) : Cuprous ion has completely filled 3d-orbitals.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Cuprous salts are diamagnetic, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason gives the cause. Copper is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1\), so \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) — formed by losing the single \(4s\) electron — is \(3d^{10}\), a completely filled subshell with every electron paired. No unpaired electron means no paramagnetism. This also explains why cuprous salts are colourless, since a full d subshell allows no d-d transition. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : n-Butyl chloride has higher boiling point than n-Butyl bromide.
Reason (R) : C – Cl bond is more polar than C – Br bond.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
n-Butyl chloride has a LOWER boiling point than n-butyl bromide, not a higher one, so the Assertion is false. Boiling point here is set by van der Waals attraction, which grows with the size and mass of the halogen; bromine is larger and more polarisable than chlorine, so the bromide boils higher.

The Reason is true — the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond IS more polar than \(\mathrm{C-Br}\), chlorine being the more electronegative — but dipole-dipole attraction is the smaller effect here and is outweighed by the van der Waals term. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Acetanilide is less basic than aniline.
Reason (R) : Acetylation of aniline results in decrease of electron density on nitrogen.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Acetanilide is less basic than aniline, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason names the cause. Acetylating the nitrogen puts a carbonyl group next to it, and that carbonyl withdraws the nitrogen lone pair by resonance onto its own oxygen. With the lone pair delocalised away from nitrogen, less electron density is available there to accept a proton, so the amide is much the weaker base. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion — and the same effect is what makes acetylation useful for controlling the nitration and bromination of aniline.

rows.stem:
Reactant ‘A’ underwent a decomposition reaction. The concentration of ‘A’ was measured periodically and recorded in the table given below :

| Time / Hours | [A]/M |
|---|---|
| 0 | \(0{\cdot}40\) |
| 1 | \(0{\cdot}20\) |
| 2 | \(0{\cdot}10\) |
| 3 | \(0{\cdot}05\) |

Based on the above data, predict the order of the reaction and write the expression for the rate law.
rows.solution:
Read the table for a pattern rather than fitting an equation. The concentration halves in each successive hour: 0.40 to 0.20 in the first hour, 0.20 to 0.10 in the second, 0.10 to 0.05 in the third. The HALF-LIFE is therefore constant at 1 hour, whatever the concentration it starts from.

A half-life independent of the starting concentration is the signature of a FIRST order reaction, for which \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\) contains no concentration term. For any other order the half-life would change as the reaction proceeded.

Order of the reaction: 1 (first order)
Rate law: \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]\)

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The reaction between \(\mathrm{H_2\,(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2\,(g)}\) was carried out in a sealed isothermal container. The rate law for the reaction was found to be :
\(\mathrm{Rate = k[H_2]\,[I_2]}\)
If 1 mole of \(\mathrm{H_2\,(g)}\) was added to the reaction chamber and the temperature was kept constant, then predict the change in rate of the reaction and the rate constant.
rows.solution:
Adding 1 mole of hydrogen to a sealed container of fixed volume raises \([\mathrm{H_2}]\). Since the rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}]\), the RATE OF THE REACTION INCREASES in proportion to that rise.

The RATE CONSTANT REMAINS THE SAME. \(k\) depends only on the temperature (through the Arrhenius equation) and on the nature of the reaction, not on how much of anything is present — and the temperature was held constant. Confusing the two is precisely what this question tests: concentration moves the rate, temperature moves the constant.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{PtCl_4 \cdot 2KCl}\) doesn't give precipitate of AgCl with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution. Write the structural formula and IUPAC name of the complex.
rows.solution:
No precipitate with silver nitrate means no free chloride ion in solution, so ALL FOUR chlorides must be inside the coordination sphere and the two potassium ions are the counter ions.

Structural formula: \(\mathrm{K_2[PtCl_6]}\)

Six chlorido ligands contribute \(-6\) and the two potassium ions \(+2\), so platinum is \(+4\). The complex is the anion, so platinum takes the \(-ate\) ending.

IUPAC name: potassium hexachloridoplatinate(IV)

rows.stem: Define fuel cell. Give two advantages of fuel cell over ordinary cell.
rows.solution:
A fuel cell is a galvanic cell in which the energy of COMBUSTION of a fuel — hydrogen, methane, methanol — is converted directly into electrical energy, the reactants being supplied continuously from outside rather than stored inside.

Two advantages over an ordinary cell:
It has a high efficiency, around 70%, because the chemical energy is converted straight to electricity rather than through heat, so it is not limited by the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine.
It is pollution free — the hydrogen-oxygen cell produces only water — and, because the reactants are fed in continuously, it runs indefinitely instead of going flat and needing replacement.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the structures of the main products of the following reactions :
(a) methyl 3-(2-oxocyclohexyl)propanoate \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaBH_4}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{6\,(CH_3)_3C\!-\!OH + 2Al \longrightarrow}\)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — sub-part (a) is a DRAWN structure and the printed stem names no compound: a cyclohexanone ring (C=O drawn at the top-left ring carbon) bearing, on the carbon ADJACENT to that carbonyl, the chain CH2CH2–C(=O)–O–CH3, with NaBH4 over the arrow. I named it losslessly as methyl 3-(2-oxocyclohexyl)propanoate; naming does not state the answer, since the question tests NaBH4's chemoselectivity between the ketone and the ester. Sub-part (b) is drawn as an expanded tert-butyl alcohol (a central C carrying two vertical CH3 bonds plus CH3 and OH) and IS typeable, so it is transcribed in line as 6 (CH3)3C-OH + 2Al. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) Sodium borohydride is a MILD reducing agent: it reduces aldehydes and ketones but NOT esters, whose carbonyl is deactivated by resonance donation from the ester oxygen. The substrate here carries a ketone on the ring and a methyl ester on the side chain, so only the ketone is attacked and the ester survives:
the product is methyl 3-(2-hydroxycyclohexyl)propanoate — the ring \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) becomes \(\mathrm{CH-OH}\) and the \(-\mathrm{CH_2CH_2COOCH_3}\) chain is unchanged.

(b) Aluminium reacts with an alcohol as it does with water, displacing hydrogen and forming the alkoxide. Each aluminium is trivalent, so it takes three tert-butoxide groups:
\(6(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-OH} + 2\mathrm{Al} \longrightarrow 2[(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O}]_3\mathrm{Al} + 3\mathrm{H_2}\)
The product is aluminium tert-butoxide.

rows.stem: What is meant by essential amino acids ? Why are amino acids amphoteric in nature ?
rows.solution:
Essential amino acids are those the body cannot synthesise for itself and which must therefore be obtained ready-made from the diet — valine, leucine and lysine among them. The rest, which the body can make, are called non-essential.

Amino acids are amphoteric because they exist as ZWITTERIONS. The \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group transfers its proton to the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group of the same molecule, giving \(\mathrm{H_3\overset{+}{N}-CHR-COO^-}\), which carries both an acidic and a basic centre. With a base the \(-\mathrm{\overset{+}{N}H_3}\) group gives up a proton, so the amino acid acts as an acid; with an acid the \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\) group accepts one, so it acts as a base.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) Allyl chloride is hydrolysed more readily than n-propyl chloride.
(ii) Isocyanides are formed when alkyl halides are treated with silver cyanide.
(iii) Methyl chloride reacts faster with \(\overline{\mathrm{O}}\mathrm{H}\) ion in \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction than t-butyl chloride.
rows.solution:
(i) Because allyl chloride can ionise to a RESONANCE-STABILISED carbocation. Losing the chloride gives the allyl cation, whose positive charge is spread over both terminal carbons through the \(\pi\) system, so it forms far more readily than the plain primary carbocation that n-propyl chloride would have to make. An easier ionisation means a faster unimolecular hydrolysis.

(ii) Because silver cyanide is largely COVALENT. The cyanide ion is ambident, able to attack through carbon or through nitrogen, but in AgCN the carbon is tied up in the bond to silver, leaving only the nitrogen lone pair free to attack. The nitrogen therefore forms the new bond and the product is the isocyanide, \(\mathrm{R-NC}\). Potassium cyanide, being ionic, frees the whole ion and attack goes through carbon, giving the alkyl cyanide instead.

(iii) Because an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction requires the nucleophile to approach the carbon from the side directly opposite the leaving group, so the LESS crowded that carbon is, the faster the reaction. Methyl chloride's carbon carries three small hydrogens and is almost unobstructed; t-butyl chloride's carries three bulky methyl groups that block the approach almost completely. Steric hindrance, not electronics, is what separates them here.

rows.stem:
Complete the following reactions by writing the structural formulae of ‘A’ and ‘B’ :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}}\) ‘A’ \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{aq.\ KOH}}\) ‘B’
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHClCH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{alc.\ KOH}}\) ‘A’ \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{HBr}}\) ‘B’
(iii) ‘A’ \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Mg}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2MgCl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^{+}}]{\mathrm{H_2O}}\) ‘B’ (Main product)
rows.solution:
(i) Hydrogen bromide in the presence of a peroxide adds ANTI-Markovnikov, so the bromine goes to the terminal carbon; aqueous potassium hydroxide then substitutes it for a hydroxyl group.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Br}\), 1-bromopropane
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\), propan-1-ol

(ii) ALCOHOLIC potassium hydroxide eliminates rather than substitutes, and by Saytzeff's rule gives the more substituted alkene; adding hydrogen bromide back follows Markovnikov's rule, so the bromine returns to the more substituted carbon.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_3}\), but-2-ene
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(Br)CH_3}\), 2-bromobutane

(iii) Magnesium in dry ether inserts into a carbon-chlorine bond to give the Grignard reagent, so the starting material must be the chloride with the same alkyl group; hydrolysis of a Grignard reagent gives the alkane.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl}\), chloroethane
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_3}\), ethane

rows.stem:
Calculate the cell voltage of the voltaic cell which is set up by joining following half-cells at \(25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) :
\(\mathrm{Al/Al^{3+}}\) \((0{\cdot}001\ \mathrm{M})\) and \(\mathrm{Ni/Ni^{2+}}\) \((0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M})\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ni^{2+}/Ni}} = -\,0{\cdot}25\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Al^{3+}/Al}} = -\,1{\cdot}66\) V
rows.solution:
Aluminium has the more negative potential, so it is the anode and nickel the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ni^{2+}/Ni}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Al^{3+}/Al}} = (-0.25) - (-1.66) = 1.41\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing electrons gives
\(2\mathrm{Al} + 3\mathrm{Ni^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Al^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Ni}\)
so six electrons are transferred and \(n = 6\).

\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Al^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}]^3}\)
\(= 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{(0.001)^2}{(0.1)^3} = 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{10^{-6}}{10^{-3}}\)
\(= 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log 10^{-3} = 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}(-3)\)
\(= 1.41 + 0.0295 = 1.4395\ \mathrm{V}\), about \(1.44\ \mathrm{V}\)

Note the logarithm is NEGATIVE here, so the correction ADDS to the standard value rather than subtracting — the sign is where this calculation is usually lost.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Give explanation for each of the following observations :
(a) With the same d-orbital configuration \((\mathrm{d^4})\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) ion is an oxidising agent whereas \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) ion is a reducing agent.
(b) Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than that among lanthanoids.
(c) Transition metals form large number of interstitial compounds with H, B, C and N.
rows.solution:
(a) Both are \(d^4\), and in each case it is the ion they BECOME that decides. \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is an oxidising agent because gaining one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly half-filled subshell of special stability — so it takes an electron readily. \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is a reducing agent because losing one electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\), a half-filled \(t_{2g}\) set, equally favourable — so it gives an electron readily. Same starting configuration, opposite behaviour, for the same kind of reason.

(b) Contraction across a series happens because the electrons being added shield the outer shells poorly, so the effective nuclear charge felt outside grows and pulls them in. The 5f orbitals of the actinoids are more diffuse and shield even less effectively than the 4f orbitals of the lanthanoids, so the effective nuclear charge rises faster from one actinoid to the next and the contraction per element is greater.

(c) Because transition metals have relatively large atoms whose crystal lattices contain sizeable interstitial voids, and the atoms of hydrogen, boron, carbon and nitrogen are small enough to fit into those voids without disturbing the lattice. The resulting interstitial compounds are non-stoichiometric, very hard, high-melting, and still metallic in conductivity — steel and cast iron being the industrially important examples.

rows.stem:
An aqueous solution of NaOH was made and its molar mass from the measurement of osmotic pressure at \(27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) was found to be 25 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\). Calculate the percentage dissociation of NaOH in this solution.
[Atomic mass : Na = 23 u, O = 16 u, H = 1 u]
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of the normal molar mass to the abnormal one:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{abnormal molar mass}}\)

Sodium hydroxide has \(M = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40\) g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), and the measurement gave 25 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\):
\(i = \dfrac{40}{25} = 1.6\)

For dissociation into \(n\) particles,
\(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1}\)
and sodium hydroxide gives two ions, so \(n = 2\):
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1.6 - 1}{2 - 1} = 0.6\)

The percentage dissociation is \(0.6 \times 100 = 60\%\).

The abnormal molar mass came out LOWER than the true one, which is the signature of dissociation: more particles than the formula suggests, so a larger colligative property and a smaller apparent mass.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following compounds as asked :
(a) in decreasing order of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NHCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)
(b) increasing order of boiling point
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\)
(c) increasing order of solubility in water
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)
rows.solution:
(a) A higher \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a weaker base, so decreasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) lists the weakest first. Aniline and N-methylaniline have nitrogen attached directly to the ring, which delocalises the lone pair and weakens them both sharply; between those two, the methyl group of N-methylaniline donates electron density and makes it the stronger. The two aliphatic amines are far stronger, and the secondary one outranks the primary. Decreasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\):
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} > \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCH_3} > \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} > (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH}\)

(b) Boiling point follows the strength of intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Dimethylamine has only ONE hydrogen on nitrogen; ethylamine has two; and ethanol has its hydrogen on OXYGEN, which is more electronegative and makes the strongest bonds of the three. Increasing boiling point:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH} < \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} < \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)

(c) Solubility in water depends on hydrogen bonding to water against the size of the hydrocarbon part. Aniline's large benzene ring makes it nearly insoluble. Diethylamine has two ethyl groups and only one hydrogen on nitrogen; ethylamine has one small ethyl group and two hydrogens, so it is the most soluble. Increasing solubility:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} < (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} < \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: An aromatic compound ‘A’ with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\) gives positive 2,4-DNP test. It gives yellow precipitate. of compound ‘B’ on treatment with sodium hypoiodite. Compound ‘A’ does not react with Tollen's or Fehling's reagent; on drastic oxidation with \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) it forms a carboxylic acid ‘C’. Elucidate the structures of A, B and C. Also give their IUPAC names.
rows.solution:
Every clue narrows the compound down. A positive 2,4-DNP test means a carbonyl group. Failing both Tollens' and Fehling's tests makes it a KETONE rather than an aldehyde. A yellow precipitate with sodium hypoiodite is the iodoform reaction, so the carbonyl carries a METHYL group. And drastic oxidation to a carboxylic acid means an aromatic ring with an oxidisable side chain. With the formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\) all of that fixes the compound as phenyl methyl ketone.

\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\), acetophenone (IUPAC: 1-phenylethan-1-one)

The yellow precipitate is iodoform, formed as the hypoiodite cleaves the methyl group away:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CHI_3}\), iodoform (IUPAC: triiodomethane)

Drastic oxidation burns the side chain back to a single carboxyl carbon on the ring:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\), benzoic acid

rows.stem:
(a) Can sodium ethoxide and t-butyl chloride be used for the preparation of t-butyl ethyl ether ? Give suitable explanation. Justify your answer by suggesting the appropriate starting material required for preparation of t-butyl ethyl ether.
(b) Give the IUPAC name of above mentioned ether.
rows.solution:
(a) No, that pairing cannot be used.

Williamson synthesis is an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, so the alkoxide must attack a LESS hindered carbon. Sodium ethoxide is a strong nucleophile but also a strong BASE, and t-butyl chloride's carbon is fully substituted and inaccessible to attack from behind. Instead of substituting, the ethoxide removes a \(\beta\) hydrogen and eliminates, giving 2-methylpropene rather than the ether.

Reversing the roles solves it: use CHLOROETHANE as the halide and SODIUM tert-BUTOXIDE as the alkoxide. The alkoxide then attacks a primary carbon, where \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) works cleanly.
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-ONa} + \mathrm{C_2H_5Cl} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

(b) The parent chain is propane with a methyl and an ethoxy group on C-2:
2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane

rows.stem: Give one example of miscible liquid pair which shows negative deviation from Raoult's law. What is the reason for such deviation ?
rows.context: According to the generally accepted definition of the ideal solution there are equal interaction forces acting between molecules belonging to the same or different species. (This is equivalent to the statement that the activity of the components equals the concentration.) Strictly speaking, this condition is fulfilled only in exceptional cases for mixtures (optical isomers, isotopic mixtures of an element, hydrocarbon mixtures). It is still usual to talk about ideal solutions as limiting cases in reality since very dilute solutions behave ideally with respect to the solvent. This view is further supported by the fact that Raoult's law empirically found for describing the behaviour of the solvent in dilute solutions can be deduced thermodynamically via the assumption of ideal behaviour of the solvent.
rows.solution:
Chloroform and acetone. Any pair whose unlike molecules attract each other more strongly than their own kind will do — nitric acid and water, or phenol and aniline, are equally good answers.

The reason for the deviation is that a NEW and STRONGER interaction appears on mixing. The hydrogen of chloroform is made unusually acidic by its three chlorine atoms, so it forms a hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen of acetone. That chloroform-to-acetone attraction is stronger than the chloroform-chloroform and acetone-acetone attractions it replaces, so after mixing the molecules are held in the liquid more tightly, fewer escape, and each partial vapour pressure falls below the value Raoult's law predicts.

rows.stem: State Raoult's law for a solution containing volatile components.
rows.context: According to the generally accepted definition of the ideal solution there are equal interaction forces acting between molecules belonging to the same or different species. (This is equivalent to the statement that the activity of the components equals the concentration.) Strictly speaking, this condition is fulfilled only in exceptional cases for mixtures (optical isomers, isotopic mixtures of an element, hydrocarbon mixtures). It is still usual to talk about ideal solutions as limiting cases in reality since very dilute solutions behave ideally with respect to the solvent. This view is further supported by the fact that Raoult's law empirically found for describing the behaviour of the solvent in dilute solutions can be deduced thermodynamically via the assumption of ideal behaviour of the solvent.
rows.solution:
Raoult's law states that for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution. For a component A,
\(p_A = p_A^{\circ}\,x_A\)
where \(p_A^{\circ}\) is the vapour pressure of pure A, and by Dalton's law the total vapour pressure is \(p = p_A^{\circ}x_A + p_B^{\circ}x_B\).

rows.stem: Raoult's law is a special case of Henry's law. Comment.
rows.context: According to the generally accepted definition of the ideal solution there are equal interaction forces acting between molecules belonging to the same or different species. (This is equivalent to the statement that the activity of the components equals the concentration.) Strictly speaking, this condition is fulfilled only in exceptional cases for mixtures (optical isomers, isotopic mixtures of an element, hydrocarbon mixtures). It is still usual to talk about ideal solutions as limiting cases in reality since very dilute solutions behave ideally with respect to the solvent. This view is further supported by the fact that Raoult's law empirically found for describing the behaviour of the solvent in dilute solutions can be deduced thermodynamically via the assumption of ideal behaviour of the solvent.
rows.solution:
Both laws say the same thing in form: the partial pressure of a component above a solution is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.
Raoult: \(p = p^{\circ}x\)
Henry: \(p = K_H\,x\)

They differ only in the proportionality constant. In Raoult's law it is \(p^{\circ}\), the vapour pressure of the pure component; in Henry's law it is \(K_H\), an empirical constant for that gas and solvent. So Raoult's law is the SPECIAL CASE of Henry's law in which \(K_H\) happens to equal \(p^{\circ}\) — which is what happens when the solute-solvent interaction is the same as the solute-solute one, that is, in an ideal solution.

rows.stem: Write two characteristics of an ideal solution.
rows.context: According to the generally accepted definition of the ideal solution there are equal interaction forces acting between molecules belonging to the same or different species. (This is equivalent to the statement that the activity of the components equals the concentration.) Strictly speaking, this condition is fulfilled only in exceptional cases for mixtures (optical isomers, isotopic mixtures of an element, hydrocarbon mixtures). It is still usual to talk about ideal solutions as limiting cases in reality since very dilute solutions behave ideally with respect to the solvent. This view is further supported by the fact that Raoult's law empirically found for describing the behaviour of the solvent in dilute solutions can be deduced thermodynamically via the assumption of ideal behaviour of the solvent.
rows.solution:
Two characteristics:
The enthalpy of mixing is zero, \(\Delta_{mix}H = 0\) — no heat is absorbed or evolved when the components are mixed, because the A-B interactions are exactly as strong as the A-A and B-B ones they replace.
The volume of mixing is zero, \(\Delta_{mix}V = 0\) — the volume of the solution equals the sum of the volumes of the components, for the same reason.

An ideal solution also obeys Raoult's law over the whole range of composition, which is the defining property from which both of these follow.

rows.stem: What products would be formed when DNA is hydrolysed ? How is DNA different from RNA with reference to a structure ?
rows.context: Ribose and 2-deoxyribose have an important role in biology. Among the most important derivatives are those with phosphate groups attached at the 5 position. Mono-, di- and tri-phosphate forms are important, as well as 3-5 cyclic monophosphates. Purines and pyrimidines form an important class of compounds with ribose and deoxyribose. When these purine and pyrimidine derivatives are coupled to a ribose sugar, they are called nucleosides.
rows.solution:
Complete hydrolysis of DNA gives its three components: the pentose sugar 2-DEOXYRIBOSE, phosphoric acid, and the nitrogenous bases — adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine.

Structurally DNA differs from RNA in being DOUBLE STRANDED: two polynucleotide chains coiled about each other in a double helix and held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs, whereas RNA is normally a single strand. The sugar differs too, 2-deoxyribose against ribose, and DNA uses thymine where RNA uses uracil.

rows.stem: Differentiate between nucleotide and nucleoside.
rows.context: Ribose and 2-deoxyribose have an important role in biology. Among the most important derivatives are those with phosphate groups attached at the 5 position. Mono-, di- and tri-phosphate forms are important, as well as 3-5 cyclic monophosphates. Purines and pyrimidines form an important class of compounds with ribose and deoxyribose. When these purine and pyrimidine derivatives are coupled to a ribose sugar, they are called nucleosides.
rows.solution:
A NUCLEOSIDE is a nitrogenous base joined to a pentose sugar: nucleoside = base + sugar.
A NUCLEOTIDE is that nucleoside further joined to phosphoric acid: nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate.

It is the nucleotide, not the nucleoside, that is the repeating unit of a nucleic acid, because the phosphate group is what links one unit to the next through the phosphodiester backbone.

rows.stem: Mention two important functions of nucleic acid.
rows.context: Ribose and 2-deoxyribose have an important role in biology. Among the most important derivatives are those with phosphate groups attached at the 5 position. Mono-, di- and tri-phosphate forms are important, as well as 3-5 cyclic monophosphates. Purines and pyrimidines form an important class of compounds with ribose and deoxyribose. When these purine and pyrimidine derivatives are coupled to a ribose sugar, they are called nucleosides.
rows.solution:
Two important functions:
Nucleic acids PRESERVE AND TRANSMIT GENETIC INFORMATION — DNA carries the hereditary information of the organism and is replicated so that each daughter cell receives a copy.
Nucleic acids DIRECT PROTEIN SYNTHESIS — the information in DNA is transcribed into RNA and translated into the amino acid sequence of proteins.

rows.stem: Name the linkage which joins two nucleotides. Name the base that is found in nucleotide of RNA but not in DNA.
rows.context: Ribose and 2-deoxyribose have an important role in biology. Among the most important derivatives are those with phosphate groups attached at the 5 position. Mono-, di- and tri-phosphate forms are important, as well as 3-5 cyclic monophosphates. Purines and pyrimidines form an important class of compounds with ribose and deoxyribose. When these purine and pyrimidine derivatives are coupled to a ribose sugar, they are called nucleosides.
rows.solution:
The linkage joining two nucleotides is the PHOSPHODIESTER linkage: a phosphate group esterified to the sugar of each of the two neighbouring nucleotides, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.

The base found in RNA but not in DNA is URACIL, which takes the place of DNA's thymine.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Complete the following reactions by writing the structure of the main products :
(I) cyclohexanone \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2NCONH\!-\!NH_2}}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2Cd + 2CH_3COCl \longrightarrow}\)
(III) benzoyl chloride \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{Pd-BaSO_4}]{\mathrm{H_2}}\)
(ii) Give simple chemical test to distinguish between the following pairs of compounds :
(I) Ethyl benzoate and benzoic acid
(II) Propanal and propanone
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — two of the three sub-parts in (i) exist only as drawn structures: (I) a cyclohexane ring with =O drawn on its right-hand vertex, with H2NCONH-NH2 over the arrow, and (III) a benzene ring bearing COCl, with H2 above the arrow and Pd-BaSO4 below it. Both were NAMED losslessly (cyclohexanone, benzoyl chloride) rather than approximated; naming does not state either answer, since the questions test what semicarbazide gives with a ketone and what Rosenmund reduction gives. Sub-part (II) is printed in line and needs no figure. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Semicarbazide condenses with the carbonyl group of cyclohexanone, losing water, so the ring \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) becomes \(\mathrm{C{=}N-NHCONH_2}\):
the product is cyclohexanone semicarbazone.

(II) A dialkyl cadmium is far less reactive than a Grignard reagent, so it stops cleanly at the ketone instead of adding twice. Each of its two methyl groups is delivered to one acyl chloride:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd} + 2\mathrm{CH_3COCl} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} + \mathrm{CdCl_2}\)
The product is propanone (acetone).

(III) Rosenmund's reduction: hydrogen over palladium poisoned with barium sulphate reduces the acyl chloride only as far as the aldehyde.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd\text{-}BaSO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
The product is benzaldehyde.

(ii)(I) Add sodium hydrogen carbonate solution. Benzoic acid is strong enough to liberate carbon dioxide and gives a brisk effervescence; ethyl benzoate is an ester, is not acidic, and gives no reaction.

(II) Use Tollens' reagent. Warmed with ammoniacal silver nitrate, propanal is oxidised and deposits a silver mirror; propanone, a ketone, gives none. The iodoform test would serve equally well the other way round.

rows.stem:
(i) Complete each synthesis by giving missing starting material, reagent or products :
(I) ethylbenzene \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ H_3O^{+}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ KMnO_4,\ KOH}}\) ?
(II) methylenecyclohexane \(\xrightarrow{?}\) cyclohexanecarbaldehyde
(III) 4-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^{+}}}\) ?
(ii) Carry out the following conversions :
(I) Benzaldehyde to Benzophenone
(II) Benzaldehyde to 3-phenyl propanol
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all three sub-parts of (i) are drawn structural schemes and the printed stem names nothing. (I) a benzene ring bearing CH2CH3, over an arrow labelled (i) KMnO4, KOH above and (ii) H3O+ below, giving '?'. (II) a cyclohexane ring with =CH2 on its right-hand vertex, an arrow labelled only '?', giving a cyclohexane ring bearing CHO. (III) a cyclohexane ring with =O on its upper-left vertex and CHO on the vertex para to it, over an arrow labelled [Ag(NH3)2]+, giving '?'. I NAMED the three drawn reactants (ethylbenzene; methylenecyclohexane; 4-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde) and, in (II) only, the drawn PRODUCT, because that product is printed as part of the question rather than as the blank — the blank in (II) is the reagent. Naming does not state any of the three answers. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Hot alkaline potassium permanganate oxidises the whole side chain of ethylbenzene back to a single carboxyl carbon, and acidification liberates the acid:
the product is benzoic acid, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\).

(II) The missing REAGENTS are asked for. Methylenecyclohexane has an exocyclic \(\mathrm{C{=}CH_2}\), and the product has a \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) on the ring carbon — so water must be added ANTI-Markovnikov, putting the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) on the terminal carbon, and that primary alcohol then oxidised without touching anything else:
\((\mathrm{BH_3})_2\); then \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}/\mathrm{OH^-}\); then PCC.

(III) Tollens' reagent is a MILD oxidant and attacks only the aldehyde group; the ring ketone is untouched, since a ketone does not reduce Tollens':
the product is the carboxylate of 4-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid — the ring keeping its \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) and the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) becoming \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\), with a silver mirror deposited.

(ii)(I) Benzaldehyde to benzophenone. Oxidise to the acid, convert to the acyl chloride, then acylate benzene:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{\mathrm{C_6H_6}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COC_6H_5}\)

(II) Benzaldehyde to 3-phenylpropanol. A crossed aldol condensation with ethanal lengthens the chain by two carbons, and catalytic hydrogenation then reduces both the double bond and the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CH_3CHO},\ \text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH{=}CHCHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2}/\mathrm{Ni}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_2CH_2OH}\)

rows.stem:
(i) Give reasons :
(I) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) is diamagnetic whereas \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) is paramagnetic. [Atomic number : Ni = 28]
(II) CO is a stronger complexing agent than \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).
(III) The trans isomer of complex \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\) is optically inactive.
(ii) Using Crystal Field theory, write the number of unpaired electrons in octahedral complexes of \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) in the presence of :
(I) Strong field ligand
(II) Weak field ligand
[Atomic number : Fe = 26]
rows.solution:
(i)(I) In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is in the ZERO oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\), and carbon monoxide is a strong field ligand: it drives the \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set so that every electron is paired, giving \(3d^{10}\) and a diamagnetic \(sp^3\) complex. In \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) nickel is \(+2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\) with two unpaired electrons, and the weak field chloride cannot force them to pair — so the complex keeps them and is paramagnetic.

(II) Because carbon monoxide bonds to the metal in BOTH directions. It donates its carbon lone pair into an empty metal orbital as a sigma bond, and it also accepts electron density back from a filled metal d orbital into its own empty \(\pi^*\) orbital. Each half of this SYNERGIC interaction strengthens the other, so the metal-carbon bond is far stronger than the simple sigma donation ammonia can offer. Ammonia has no empty orbital of the right symmetry to accept back-donation at all.

(III) Because the trans isomer has a PLANE OF SYMMETRY. With the two chlorido ligands opposite each other, the molecule can be divided into two mirror-image halves, so it is superimposable on its own mirror image and therefore optically inactive. The CIS isomer has no such plane and is optically active — which is why the question specifies trans.

(ii) Iron is \(+3\), so \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\).
(I) With a STRONG field ligand, \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\), so the electrons pair as far as they can into the lower \(t_{2g}\) set: \(t_{2g}^5 e_g^0\), leaving ONE unpaired electron.
(II) With a WEAK field ligand, \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\), so no pairing occurs and all five orbitals are singly occupied: \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^2\), leaving FIVE unpaired electrons — the maximum possible.

rows.stem:
(i) Name the type of isomerism exhibited by the following compounds. Also draw their corresponding isomers.
(I) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]\,[Cr(CN)_6]}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\)
(III) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]}\)
(ii) Differentiate between weak field and strong field ligands. How does the strength of the ligand influence the spin of the complex ?
rows.solution:
(i)(I) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6][Cr(CN)_6]}\) shows COORDINATION ISOMERISM. Both ions are complexes, so the ligand sets can be exchanged between the two metal centres. Its isomer is
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6][Co(CN)_6]}\)

(II) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) shows OPTICAL ISOMERISM. Three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands wrap round the cobalt in a propeller with no plane of symmetry, so the ion exists as two non-superimposable mirror images — the \(d\) and \(l\) forms, drawn as an octahedron and its reflection with the three chelate rings twisting the opposite way.

(III) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]}\) shows GEOMETRICAL ISOMERISM. With three of each ligand on an octahedron there are two arrangements: the FACIAL isomer, in which the three ammine ligands occupy one triangular face and the three nitro groups the opposite one, and the MERIDIONAL isomer, in which each set of three lies along a meridian of the octahedron.

(ii) A WEAK field ligand produces a small crystal field splitting; a STRONG field ligand produces a large one. The spectrochemical series arranges ligands by that strength, running from iodide and bromide at the weak end through water and ammonia to cyanide and carbon monoxide at the strong end.

The strength decides the spin because it is compared against the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\). When \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\), promoting an electron to the upper set costs less than pairing, so the electrons spread out and the complex is HIGH SPIN with the maximum number of unpaired electrons. When \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\), pairing is the cheaper option, so the lower set fills first and the complex is LOW SPIN, with fewer unpaired electrons and often diamagnetic.

rows.stem:
(i) The initial concentration of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) in the first order reaction :
\(\mathrm{N_2O_5\,(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{2NO_2\,(g)} + \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{O_2\,(g)}\)
was \(1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-2}\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\). The concentration of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) after 60 minutes was \(0{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-2}\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\). Calculate the rate constant of the reaction at 318 K.
[log 6 = \(0{\cdot}778\)]
(ii) Account for the following :
(I) We cannot determine the order of a reaction by taking into consideration the balanced chemical equation.
(II) A bimolecular reaction may become kinetically of first order under a specified condition.
rows.solution:
(i) For a first order reaction,
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

With \([\mathrm{R}]_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\), \([\mathrm{R}] = 0.2 \times 10^{-2}\) and \(t = 60\) min,
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{60}\log\dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-2}}{0.2 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{2.303}{60}\log 6 = \dfrac{2.303}{60} \times 0.778\)
\(k = 2.98 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

The unit is minutes\(^{-1}\) because the time was given in minutes; the ratio of concentrations is dimensionless, so nothing else enters.

(ii)(I) Because order is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity and the balanced equation describes only the net change, not the mechanism. Most reactions proceed through several steps, and the observed rate is set by the slowest of them, which may involve species and proportions quite different from those in the overall equation — a catalyst, for instance, appears in the rate law but not in the equation. Order can even be zero or fractional, which no stoichiometric coefficient could produce.

(II) When one of the two reactants is present in LARGE EXCESS. Its concentration then barely changes as the reaction proceeds and can be absorbed into the rate constant, so rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\) becomes rate \(= k'[\mathrm{A}]\). The reaction is still bimolecular in mechanism but first order in kinetics — a pseudo first order reaction, of which the acid hydrolysis of an ester in dilute aqueous solution is the standard example.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(i) The rate of the chemical reaction doubles for an increase of 10 K in absolute temperature from 298 K. Calculate activation energy \((\mathrm{E_a})\).
[\(2{\cdot}303\) R = \(19{\cdot}15\) \(\mathrm{JK^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\), log 2 = \(0{\cdot}3\)]
(ii) For a reaction :
\(\mathrm{2H_2O_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{I^{-}}} \mathrm{2H_2O + O_2}\)
the proposed mechanism is as given below :
(I) \(\mathrm{H_2O_2 + I^{-} \longrightarrow H_2O + IO^{-}}\) (slow)
(II) \(\mathrm{H_2O_2 + IO^{-} \longrightarrow H_2O + I^{-} + O_2}\) (fast)
(1) Write rate law for the reaction.
(2) Write the overall order and molecularity of the reaction.
rows.solution:
(i) Use the two-temperature Arrhenius equation, with \(T_1 = 298\) K and \(T_2 = 308\) K and the rate doubling, so \(k_2/k_1 = 2\):
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right]\)
\(\log 2 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15}\left[\dfrac{10}{298 \times 308}\right]\)
\(0.3 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15} \times \dfrac{10}{298 \times 308}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.3 \times 19.15 \times 298 \times 308}{10}\)
\(E_a = 52729\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(52.729\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The question gives \(2.303\,R\) already multiplied out as \(19.15\), which is worth noticing before multiplying by \(R\) a second time.

(ii)(1) The rate of a multi-step reaction is set by its slowest step, and only the species appearing in that step enter the rate law. Step (I) consumes one \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) and one \(\mathrm{I^-}\), so
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{H_2O_2}][\mathrm{I^-}]\)

(2) Reading the exponents off that expression, the overall ORDER is \(1 + 1 = 2\). The MOLECULARITY of the rate-determining step is likewise 2 — bimolecular, since one molecule and one ion collide.

Note that the iodide ion does not appear in the overall balanced equation at all: it is regenerated in step (II) and acts as a catalyst. Yet it appears in the rate law, which is exactly why order must be measured rather than read off the equation.
